promptText: A team wants every Money record to reject a negative amount, no matter which code path constructs it (including a JSON deserializer calling the constructor via reflection). Where should that check live?
options: In the compact constructor, since it is the one choke point every construction path, including reflective ones, must pass through
In a static factory method like Money.of(...), since factories are the only place validation can throw
In the accessor method amount(), since that is what callers actually read
In an @PostConstruct-annotated method on the record
explanation: A compact constructor runs for every possible construction path, including reflection-based deserialization frameworks, making it the unavoidable place to validate. A static factory only protects callers who go through that factory method, and records have no @PostConstruct lifecycle hook or setter-style validation on accessors.

promptText: Why can a Java record never extend another (non-record) class?
options: Every record implicitly extends java.lang.Record already, and Java has no multiple class inheritance
Extending a class would silently corrupt the compiler-generated equals()/hashCode(), so the language forbids it for that reason alone
A record may extend exactly one other class, but only if that class is itself declared as a record
Records are compiled as interfaces internally, and interfaces cannot extend classes
explanation: Every record implicitly extends java.lang.Record, and since Java lacks multiple class inheritance, there's no room for a second superclass; a record can still implement any number of interfaces. This is a permanent structural fact about records, not a side effect of equals()/hashCode() generation or a special case for record-to-record inheritance (which is also not allowed).

promptText: A record has a single component declared as `int[] values`. What is the consequence for the compiler-generated equals() method?
options: Two records with different array instances holding equal contents will compare as unequal, since arrays compare by reference
The compiler automatically calls Arrays.equals() on array components since it detects the array type
The record fails to compile because arrays are not allowed as components
equals() always returns false for any record containing an array component, even when compared to itself
explanation: The generated equals() compares each component using its own equals() semantics; arrays don't override equals() in Java at all, so array components are compared by reference identity, not contents. The compiler does NOT special-case arrays to call Arrays.equals() -- the fix is to use List instead of an array, or override equals()/hashCode() explicitly.

promptText: What does `sealed` do to a type hierarchy in modern Java?
options: Restricts which classes/interfaces may implement or extend it to an explicit, author-controlled permits list
Requires every permitted subtype to itself be declared as a record
Makes every method in the type implicitly final
Automatically generates equals() and hashCode() for the sealed type and all its subtypes
explanation: Sealed types restrict extension to an explicit permits list (or subtypes declared in the same file), which is what enables exhaustive switch checking. A common misconception is that every permitted subtype must be a record -- in fact a sealed hierarchy can freely mix records with plain final classes, and exhaustiveness checking doesn't care which kind each subtype is.

promptText: Given `sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Rectangle, Triangle {}` with all three permitted types implemented as records, what happens if a switch expression over a Shape variable has a case for each of the three types but no default branch?
options: It compiles successfully because the compiler proves the switch is exhaustive over the sealed hierarchy
It fails to compile because every switch expression must have a default case regardless of sealing
It compiles but throws MatchException at runtime if an unhandled subtype ever appears
It compiles only if the cases are ordered alphabetically by type name
explanation: Because Shape is sealed with exactly three permitted subtypes, the compiler can verify a case exists for each one and accepts the switch as exhaustive with no default required. Adding a fourth permitted subtype later without updating the switch causes a compile error, not a deferred runtime MatchException, which is precisely the point of exhaustiveness checking.

promptText: In `if (!(obj instanceof String s)) { return; } System.out.println(s.length());`, why is `s` legally usable after the if block, even though it was declared inside the if's condition?
options: Flow scoping: the compiler proves the only way to reach the line after the if is when the pattern matched, since the negated branch returns
Pattern variables declared in an instanceof check are always promoted to method-level scope regardless of control flow
The negation operator (!) implicitly converts the pattern variable into a field on the enclosing class
This only compiles because s happens to also be declared as a local variable earlier in the method
explanation: Flow scoping means the pattern variable's scope extends wherever definite assignment analysis can prove the type test held; here, the only way to reach the line after the if is if the instanceof matched (since the negated branch returns). It is a compiler-checked guarantee tied to that specific control flow, not a blanket promotion to method scope.

promptText: What new capability does a record pattern like `case Point(int x, int y) ->` add beyond a plain type pattern like `case Point p ->`?
options: It deconstructs the record into its components in the same step, binding x and y directly instead of requiring p.x() and p.y() calls
It is functionally identical to the type pattern, just a slightly shorter way to write the same type check
It allows the same case to match several unrelated, non-record types at once
It replaces the need for the enclosing type to be sealed for exhaustiveness to work
explanation: A record pattern both tests the type and deconstructs it into named component variables in one step, and this nests arbitrarily deeply for nested records, replacing chains of accessor calls. It is not merely cosmetic syntax sugar over the type pattern, since it genuinely eliminates the need to call accessors, and it has no bearing on how many types a case can match or on exhaustiveness rules for sealed types.

promptText: Which of the following is NOT a valid use of `var` in modern Java?
options: Declaring a field's type: `var count;` inside a class body
A local variable with an initializer: `var list = new ArrayList<String>();`
A traditional for-loop index: `for (var i = 0; i < 10; i++)`
A try-with-resources variable: `try (var in = new FileInputStream(f))`
explanation: var is restricted to local variables with an initializer and cannot be used for fields, method parameters/return types, or catch parameters, since there's no guaranteed initializer to infer the type from at those sites. Local variables, for-loop indices, and try-with-resources variables are all valid, well-established uses.

promptText: A virtual thread executes a slow network call inside a `synchronized` block. A teammate suggests fixing the resulting scalability regression by simply removing the synchronized keyword entirely, without any replacement. Why is that risky, and what is the recommended fix instead?
options: Removing synchronized without replacement loses the mutual-exclusion guarantee entirely; replacing it with java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock preserves exclusion while still letting the virtual thread unmount while blocked
The fix is correct as stated: virtual threads never need explicit locking because the JVM schedules them cooperatively
synchronized should be replaced with ThreadLocal, which allows safe unmounting during blocking calls
The regression is unrelated to synchronized; it is actually caused by the network call being too slow, which no code change can fix
explanation: The pinning problem is that synchronized prevents the JVM from unmounting a blocked virtual thread from its carrier; simply deleting synchronized would remove the mutual-exclusion protection the code actually needs for correctness. ReentrantLock provides the same exclusion guarantee but is implemented in a way that lets the virtual thread unmount while blocked, fixing the scalability issue without sacrificing thread safety; ThreadLocal is unrelated to locking or pinning.

promptText: What guarantee does `StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure` provide when three subtasks are forked and one of them fails?
options: It cancels the remaining subtasks and propagates the failure via throwIfFailed(), giving all-or-nothing semantics
It ignores the failure and returns whatever partial results the successful subtasks produced
It automatically retries only the failed subtask, up to a configurable number of attempts
It silently logs the failure and continues waiting for all subtasks to finish normally before returning
explanation: ShutdownOnFailure cancels sibling subtasks the instant any one subtask fails and propagates that failure via throwIfFailed(), giving clean all-or-nothing semantics without manual cancellation wiring. It does not silently continue, auto-retry, or return partial results -- that behavior belongs to a different joiner policy entirely (or a custom one).

promptText: In the 'sealed + records + pattern matching = algebraic data types' framing, what role does a sealed interface play, and how does that differ from the record's role?
options: The sealed interface is the sum type (this value is exactly one of these alternatives); the record is the product type (a fixed tuple of fields present at once)
The sealed interface is the product type bundling fields together, while the record is the sum type enumerating alternatives
Both the sealed interface and the record express the same sum-type concept; they are interchangeable in this framing
The sealed interface generates equals()/hashCode() for all its permitted subtypes, which is what makes the pairing an ADT
explanation: A sealed interface is the sum type (an enumeration of the closed set of alternatives a value can be), while a record is the product type (a fixed tuple of fields, all present at once) -- swapping these roles is a common mix-up. Sealing does not generate equals/hashCode for its subtypes; that generation is a record-specific feature unrelated to sealing.

promptText: A developer argues that a JPA entity could be converted to a record as long as every field is annotated with the correct JPA column mappings. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
options: Annotations don't solve the structural problems: records lack a no-arg constructor, are implicitly final (blocking lazy-loading proxy subclassing), and generate field-based equals() instead of identifier-based equality
JPA annotations cannot be placed on record components at all, so the code would fail to compile
Records only support a maximum of three fields, which is too few for most entities
Hibernate specifically detects and rejects any class named with the word 'record' in its type hierarchy
explanation: The blockers are structural, not about annotation coverage: JPA needs a no-arg constructor for reflective instantiation, mutable fields for lazy-loading proxies (which subclass the entity -- impossible since records are final), and identifier-based equality, none of which annotations can retrofit onto a record. Records can have annotations on components just fine (e.g., Bean Validation), so 'missing annotations' was never the actual issue.

promptText: A developer replaces a ThreadLocal<String> used for request correlation IDs with a ScopedValue<String>, expecting identical behavior. What is the key semantic difference they need to account for?
options: ScopedValue has no set()/remove() at all -- the binding is immutable once established via where(...).run(...) and is automatically gone when that call returns, so any code relying on mutating the value mid-request must be redesigned
ScopedValue works identically to ThreadLocal but simply runs faster, with no behavioral differences to account for
ScopedValue can only be used with platform threads, so the migration would break on virtual threads
ScopedValue requires calling remove() explicitly in a finally block, exactly like ThreadLocal, or the binding leaks
explanation: ScopedValue bindings are immutable once set via where(...).run(...)/call(...), with no set() method at all, and the binding's lifetime is lexically tied to that invocation -- so any code pattern that mutates a ThreadLocal mid-request has no direct equivalent and must be redesigned. It was specifically designed to be cheap and safe at virtual-thread scale (the opposite of being restricted to platform threads), and it cannot leak by construction, so no manual remove() is needed.

promptText: Which JVM Flight Recorder (JFR) event is specifically emitted to help diagnose virtual thread carrier-pinning issues in production with low overhead?
options: jdk.VirtualThreadPinned
jdk.GCHeapSummary
jdk.ThreadStart
jdk.ExecutionSample
explanation: The JVM emits a jdk.VirtualThreadPinned event whenever a virtual thread blocks while pinned to its carrier, recording duration and a stack trace, and JFR can run continuously in production with low overhead. jdk.GCHeapSummary, jdk.ThreadStart, and jdk.ExecutionSample are real JFR events too, but they report heap sizing, thread creation, and CPU sampling respectively -- none of them are the dedicated pinning diagnostic.

promptText: A codebase has a PaymentMethod hierarchy that third-party plugin authors are expected to extend with their own payment types, and the codebase adds new operations over payment types only rarely. According to the chapter's 'expression problem' framing, should this hierarchy be sealed with pattern-matching switches, or left as open polymorphism?
options: Left as open polymorphism, since the hierarchy must stay open for unknown third-party implementers, and cases (implementations) will grow far more often than operations
Sealed with pattern-matching switches, since sealing always produces more maintainable code regardless of extensibility requirements
Sealed with pattern-matching switches, because sealing is required to enable dependency injection of plugin implementations
Left as open polymorphism only because sealing would prevent the classes from implementing any interfaces at all
explanation: Sealed types plus exhaustive pattern matching optimize for a fixed, closed set of cases where new operations are added often; a plugin SPI is the textbook opposite shape, an open hierarchy where cases (implementations) grow and are authored by code the team doesn't control, so traditional polymorphism is the right fit here. Sealing has nothing to do with dependency injection, and it does not prevent implementing interfaces -- the issue is specifically that sealing would reject any implementer not named in the permits clause, breaking the plugin model.
